name: Trung / Dulong
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

catalog_locator: Perlin 2019 ch. 2 'Stress and Rhythm' pp. 59-60 and 'Tone' pp. 60-61; ch. 3 p. 69 (phonological word). LaPolla 2017 draft section 2 (Phonology), p. 2 of PDF.
catalog_quote: In disyllabic words, which make up most of the lexicon, Trung is a strongly sesquisyllabic (“one-and-a-half syllable”) language, featuring an unstressed presyllable followed by a stressed main syllable. This “iambic” pattern is very much in keeping with other Tibeto-Burman languages and languages of Southeast Asia. ... One statistical analysis of a small Trung lexicon (Dai and Liu 1987) found that some 87% of all disyllabic words have a reduced first syllable. ... Compounds with three syllables ... may have a reduced syllable in any position, depending on the compound’s constituent parts ... Fixed four-syllable phrases (and compounds) ... typically reduce the first and third syllables, as expected. ... Grammatical particles and affixes are generally unstressed, resulting in a disyllabic word with stress on the initial syllable and a less typical trochaic pattern, e.g. ɛt⁵⁵ɕɯ³¹ ‘laugh’. …

audit.reasoning: Quote check: all segments of the deciding quotation, the domain quotation and the exceptions quotation were found verbatim in the Perlin 2019 text we hold at the stated printed pages (59-61, 69), and the LaPolla 2017 cross-check passage is verbatim at p. 2 of the held draft. The deciding source is a 457-page 2019 reference grammar with an explicit stress section, the best item in Glottolog's list, corroborated by an independent specialist sketch (LaPolla 2017): both describe a two-tone system with toneless reduced syllables and stress determined by syllable type (full vs reduced) in a sesquisyllabic/iambic word shape, which is exactly what the record codes (classification tonal, no positional stress rule, trisyllables with 'nearly equal stress' on the two full syllables).

sources.note: Historical-phonology comparison of Dulong with Proto-Tibeto-Burman; expected to reproduce the Dulong phoneme and tone inventory (after Sun 1982: 55, 53 and the 31 of weak syllables) and to discuss whether Dulong tones correspond to anything reconstructible, i.e. the low functional load / secondary origin of Dulong tone. sources.note: Per the search-result description of Straub's translation, the sketch gives the phonology of southern Dulong: 39 initials, 120 rimes, non-distinctive aspiration, and three vowel lengths (long, half-long, short); ZMYYC sketches state the tone inventory with pitch values for each language, so this is a first-hand tone inventory for the Muliwang variety (expected: high level 55, high falling 53 and the low falling 31 of weak syllables, as in Liu 1989). Not downloaded: tone statement already listed here.
